decisions.reason: After several years without visible follow-through and given its narrow particle-therapy niche and initially incomplete rollout, management would likely judge performance as falling short of aspiration and reallocate resources.

Despite the lack of later visibility, this small-volume ionization chamber remains close to the firm's core dosimetry business, so boundedly rational management would more likely retain it while monitoring demand and fit within the portfolio.

Because it overlaps with other chamber offerings and has no clear later market signal, its risk of withdrawal is elevated, but organizational slack and core technological fit still make continued offering slightly more likely than exit.

A standard clinical ionization chamber line sits squarely in the firm's central competence and customer workflow, so management would usually keep it unless there were clear evidence of persistent underperformance.

This relative-dosimetry chamber serves a narrower use case, which raises the chance of falling below aspiration, but it still supports the firm's established radiotherapy QA portfolio and would likely be retained for now.
A thimble ionization chamber is a conventional and complementary product for the firm's customer base, so even with limited public visibility management would tend to keep it in the catalogue.
